newsitem.title: FRANCE: Immigration reform inches through French assembly.
newsitem.headline: Immigration reform inches through French assembly.

text.p: French parliamentarians waded through a sea of amendments to a hotly disputed immigration reform bill on Thursday but leaders of the centre-right majority predicted it would be approved before midnight.

Opposition Socialists, who have demanded the bill's withdrawal, accused the conservative government of quietly introducing a new database of French citizens under the pretext of monitoring visitors from developing countries.

"Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre has said there would be a register of visitors. There will necessarily be some form of control of hosts," Socialist former prime minister Laurent Fabius told RTL radio.

The government, which previously denied any register would be set up, acknowledged during a third day of rowdy National Assembly debate on the bill that records would be kept of visitors staying in France.
The bill aims to close loopholes in tough existing laws dating from 1993 and would grant the police extended powers to track immigrants in France.
The leftist opposition says the government is pandering to the growing numbers of voters for the extreme-right National Front with an eye on general elections in 1998.

It has proposed dozens of amendments in hopes of slowing or derailing the bill but eventual passage seems assured as the centre-right holds four-fifths of the assembly's 577 seats. The bill would then return to the Senate for further debate.
The Socialists, France's biggest opposition force, have sought the spotlight after initial opposition to the bill was spearheaded by film-makers, artists and intellectuals.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin has now pledged to abolish the measure if his party wins general elections due in March next year.
The Association of University Presidents jumped into the fray by approving a motion at its annual conference urging France to retain policies favouring open international educational exchanges.
During Wednesday's session, Gaullist assembly speaker Philippe Seguin had to intervene several times to urge calm.
Most amendments were thrown out but was approved allowing illegal immigrants who have been in France for more than 15 years to obtain residence permits.
The provision had been in the bill as drafted by the government but was knocked out by Senate hardliners during its first reading of the measure.
Also approved was a key article authorising police to keep the passports or travel documents of illegal immigrants and allowing searches of commercial vehicles within 20 km (12 miles) of the border.
The article also authorises police to take the fingerprints of foreigners from outside the European Union who apply for a residence permit.

Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said he would ask other European Union foreign ministers to consider reining in the European Parliament after it approved a motion urging France to drop the immigration bill.
He said he wanted his fellow ministers "to reflect on the European Parliament's exceeding its responsibilities."
